(Sonal messages her friend Mridul an hour before her first client presentation.)
Sonal: my hands are cold. what if I fumble a number in front of the whole client team
Mridul: ok quick test. last month's review, Sumit mixed up two slides. what exactly did he get wrong?
Sonal: ...no idea actually
Sonal: I just remember being nervous about my own part
Mridul: exactly 😄 everyone's in their own head
Sonal: hmm. so if I trip on a number, they'll mostly be thinking about their next question
Mridul: or their lunch
Sonal: ok. new rule for myself: I'm allowed one fumble. I'll correct it and move on
Mridul: go get them 👍
(Two hours later)
Sonal: fumbled a percentage. corrected it. nobody even blinked 🙂

qa.a: Sumit might feel relieved, and perhaps freer the next time he presents.

In the panchayat hall at Rampura, the ceiling fan clicked on every turn. Amandeep, twenty-four and three months into her job as the block's farm extension officer, had to explain the new drip-irrigation scheme to forty farmers. Her Punjabi was fine; her notes were fine. Her stomach was not.
She thought of last month's meeting, when Jatin, her senior, had called the scheme by the wrong year. What had the farmers done? She tried to remember. Nothing. Old Harbans ji had been asking about fertiliser the whole time.
They're thinking about their own fields, she told herself. Not my grammar.
She stood up. Halfway through, she read a date wrong, laughed, fixed it, and went on. At the end, three farmers crowded round to ask about their own plots.

qa.q: How many farmers did Amandeep have to explain the scheme to?
qa.a: She had to explain it to forty farmers.

qa.q: What does Amandeep's thought 'They're thinking about their own fields' show?
qa.a: It shows she has realised the farmers are focused on their own worries, which lets her feel she can speak without being perfect. 🙂

qa.q: What choice did Amandeep make when she read a date wrong, and how did it help?
qa.a: She laughed, fixed it and went on, which kept the slip small and the meeting on track.

qa.q: How did the meeting look to the three farmers who crowded round at the end?
qa.a: They cared about their own plots and the scheme, not a wrong date, so the slip probably never registered with them.

grounding: A young extension officer recalls how little anyone noticed a senior's slip and lets herself speak imperfectly.

passage:
Mei had been dreading the Friday stand-up at the Melbourne office for a week. English was her second language, and she was sure a wrong word would follow her around the office kitchen for days.
On Thursday night she tried an experiment. She wrote down every mistake she remembered colleagues making in meetings that month. The list had one line: Felix said "Tuesday" when he meant "Thursday". She couldn't even remember which meeting it was.
If that was all she had kept from a month of other people talking, how much would they keep of hers?
At stand-up she spoke for two minutes, mixed up "borrow" and "lend" once, heard it, and kept going. Afterwards Felix asked where she had bought her coffee. That was all anyone said.

qa.q: What was the only line on Mei's list of colleagues' mistakes?
qa.a: Felix said "Tuesday" when he meant "Thursday".

qa.q: What did Mei realise from her one-line list?
qa.a: Mei felt reassured, realising she keeps almost nothing of other people's slips, so her colleagues are probably too busy with themselves to keep hers.

qa.q: Which choice during stand-up showed Mei had given herself permission to be imperfect?
qa.a: When she mixed up "borrow" and "lend", she heard it and kept going instead of freezing.

qa.q: Why might Felix ask about Mei's coffee rather than her slip?
qa.a: Felix was probably thinking about his own morning, not grading Mei's English, so the slip never stood out to him.

grounding: A young professional lists the colleagues' slips she remembers, finds almost none, and speaks at stand-up without needing perfection.

The cricket final on TV was in its last over when the power went out. Tanvir groaned and grabbed his phone to check the score, but the signal kept dropping.
Five-year-old Sudha ran to the kitchen and came back holding the steel spoon she always held during matches. She squeezed it with both hands and shut her eyes tight. "If I don't let go, we win," she said.
Tanvir finally got the score. "We won!"
Sudha opened her eyes and hugged the spoon. "I did it."
Tanvir laughed and let her keep the credit.

qa.q: Why did Sudha squeeze the spoon with her eyes shut during the power cut?

qa.a: He could ask playfully whether children on the other side were holding spoons too, and say cheering is fun even though spoons don't decide scores.

On the terrace of their Chennai flat, Shankar watched the colony boys' cricket match below. His team, the Blue Stars, were losing. Shankar, five, pulled off his T-shirt, turned it inside out and put it back on.
"Why inside out?" asked his appa, Lokesh.
"So they win."
Two wickets fell. Shankar hopped on one foot. The Blue Stars hit a four, and he hopped faster. When they lost anyway, he looked down at his foot, puzzled.
Lokesh sat down beside him. "Want to hop for the next match too?"
"Yes. Harder," Shankar said.

qa.q: What did Shankar do to his T-shirt?
qa.a: He turned it inside out and put it back on.

qa.q: What does Shankar's plan to hop 'harder' next time suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he still believes his actions steer the match, and feeling in charge is more comforting than accepting he can't change it.

qa.q: How could Lokesh support Shankar without mocking the ritual?
qa.a: He could enjoy the hopping with him but also point to what the players did, like hitting the four, so Shankar sees who really plays the game.

qa.q: How might the Blue Stars players feel if they knew about Shankar's hopping?
qa.a: They would probably be touched to have such a keen fan, even though their own batting and bowling decided the match.

grounding: A small boy turns his shirt inside out and hops, believing it will make his colony team win.

It was pouring, the school bus was twenty minutes late, and the maths exam started at nine. Aditi dug through her bag for the third time. The blue pen with the chewed cap, the one she had used for every test since Class 3, wasn't there.
"I'll fail," she said, and her voice wobbled.
Ishita held out a pen. "Take mine. It writes the same."
"It's not the same." Aditi's hands were cold. On the bus she kept counting: every test with the blue pen, good marks. Every time without... she couldn't remember a time without.
In the exam hall she wrote her name with Ishita's pen, very slowly. Then she read the first question and knew the answer.

qa.q: What was special about the pen Aditi couldn't find?
qa.a: It was the blue pen with the chewed cap, used for every test since Class 3.

qa.q: Why did Aditi's voice wobble when she said 'I'll fail'?
qa.a: Aditi felt scared because she truly believed the blue pen helped her score well, so losing it on a rushed, rainy morning felt like losing her luck. 😰

qa.q: What turning point in the exam hall could help Aditi trust herself instead of the pen?
qa.a: Knowing the first answer with Ishita's pen shows the maths was in her head, not in the pen; noticing that could loosen the routine's grip.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel when Aditi says 'It's not the same'?
qa.a: Ishita might feel a little brushed off, since the offer was kind, but also worried at seeing a friend's cold hands and wobbly voice.

grounding: A girl who loses her lucky pen on exam morning feels real panic, sure the pen decides her marks.

Before every under-12 match at the Kothrud ground, Lalit did the same things: left shoe first, three taps of the bat on the crease, and the corner seat on the team bench. He had scored fifty once after that routine, and since then he never skipped it.
On Saturday, Santosh got to the bench first and sat in the corner seat, swinging his legs.
"That's my seat," Lalit said.
"Seats aren't anyone's," said Santosh.
Lalit sat at the other end, knee bouncing. He tied his right shoe first by mistake and had to undo it. When he walked out to bat, his mouth was dry.

qa.q: What could Lalit's coach help him try before the next match?
qa.a: The coach could help him build a routine about skills, like watching the bowler's hand and breathing slowly, which works from any seat.

qa.q: How might Santosh see Lalit's glare at the corner seat?
qa.a: Santosh just sat where there was space, so the glare might feel confusing and unfair to him.

passage:
Seema mole, you think you're lucky with numbers? Let me tell you about your Jomon Chachan at sixteen.
Every year at the church feast in our village there was a lucky draw, first prize a bicycle. Tickets were printed in order, but I made the seller let me choose. I would sit in the shade for an hour doing sums with my birth date, my house number, the day of the week. I was sure my number, chosen with so much effort, was stronger than a ticket someone just grabbed.
Three years running I chose. Three years running someone who grabbed won. Once it was my little cousin, who couldn't even read numbers yet.
I still remember her dancing next to that bicycle she couldn't ride. That day I finally understood: the drum doesn't care who thought hardest.

qa.q: What was the first prize at the church feast draw?
qa.a: First prize was a bicycle.

qa.q: Why did young Jomon believe his ticket was stronger?
qa.a: He had put an hour of sums and effort into choosing it, and that effort made his number feel as if it deserved to win more than a grabbed ticket.

qa.q: What was the turning point that changed Jomon's thinking?
qa.a: Seeing his little cousin, who couldn't even read numbers, win with a grabbed ticket showed him that effort had no hold on the draw.

qa.q: How might Seema use this story the next time a number feels lucky?
qa.a: Seema might laugh, then remember that the drum doesn't care who thought hardest, and be slower to trust a chosen number.

grounding: An uncle recalls believing, at sixteen, that a carefully chosen ticket beat random ones, until a small child's grabbed ticket won.

The school carnival was closing in twenty minutes, and Imran, fourteen, had exactly fifty rupees left: his bus fare home. At the scratch-card table a teacher was calling, "Last cards, win a football!"
Imran ran his fingers over the pile, lifting one, putting it back. "This one feels right," he said. "If I pick carefully, I'll get it."
His sister Parveen tugged his sleeve. "That's the bus money."

qa.q: What was it like for Parveen, watching Imran at the table?
qa.a: Parveen was probably worried about getting home, and could see clearly what Imran couldn't in that moment: the prize was already fixed on one card.

passage:
Last year, in my second year of college, I was sure I had cracked it. I'm Harsh, and I had watched hours of videos about chart patterns on a video site. I drew lines on price graphs of small company shares in a trading app and called it my system.
The first week I made a little. Then I lost. My system said the price had to bounce, so I put in double to win it back. It dropped again. I doubled again. Each loss felt like proof I was close, like a puzzle I almost had.
My friends Disha and Mehak noticed I had stopped coming to the canteen. "Bhai, you look like you haven't slept," Disha said. Mehak was blunter: "You've lost your whole scholarship money, Harsh. That's not a system."
I was angry for a day. Then I showed my parents the screen, and we went to the college counsellor together.

qa.q: What did Harsh call the lines he drew on price graphs?
qa.a: He called it his system.

qa.q: Why did each loss feel to Harsh like proof he was close?
qa.a: Believing in his system made losses look like near misses in a puzzle he could solve, so doubling felt clever rather than risky.

qa.q: What was the turning point that stopped Harsh's losses from growing?
qa.a: Mehak naming the loss plainly, and Harsh then choosing to show his parents and see the counsellor, broke the cycle.

qa.q: How did Disha and Mehak experience Harsh's 'system' from the outside?
qa.a: They saw a friend vanish from the canteen and stop sleeping, which worried them enough to step in.

grounding: A young man believes his chart system will beat random price swings and keeps doubling after losses until friends step in.

Counsellor's notes, college wellness centre (Devika)
Wasim, 20, came in today after his roommate insisted. He talked fast about an online card game. He is sure he has a method: watch three rounds, then bet on the fourth. He showed me a notebook full of tallies. "I'm just unlucky this month. The method works. I only need to win back what I lost, then I'll stop."
He has lost his semester's hostel fees. Each time he lost, he says, he raised the stake "to fix it faster".
I didn't argue about probability. I asked how much he had slept this week, and how it felt to hide the notebook from his family. He went quiet, then said, "Tired."
Next steps: he agreed to a second session on Friday, to block the app with his roommate's help, and to think about telling his elder brother. I gave him details of a support group for gambling problems.

qa.q: What was Wasim's method in the card game?
qa.a: Watch three rounds, then bet on the fourth.

qa.q: Why does 'I only need to win back what I lost' feel reasonable to Wasim?
qa.a: His tallies make him feel in control, so losses look like temporary bad luck that his method will soon correct.

qa.q: Why was Devika's choice not to argue about probability a wise one?
qa.a: Asking about sleep and the hidden notebook reached how Wasim actually felt, which opened the door to real next steps instead of a debate.

qa.q: How might Wasim's roommate see the last few weeks?
qa.a: The roommate likely watched Wasim grow tired and secretive, and cared enough to push him to the wellness centre.

grounding: A counsellor notes a young man sure his betting method will win back his losses, raising the stakes after each one.

Dear Seema,
You asked why I stopped wearing the "lucky" green dupatta to the Sunday market. Here's the honest answer.
After three bad Sundays in a row, I sat down with a notebook and split a page in two. Left side: what I control. Recipes, fresh stock, a clear price board, being there on time, talking to customers. Right side: what I don't. Rain. A wedding in the next lane pulling the crowd away. Whatever mood people wake up in.
I put all my effort into the left side. New cardamom buns, a bigger board. The right side I let be. When it rained last week and I sold half, I didn't blame the dupatta, and I didn't blame myself.
Sales are better overall. Some Sundays are still bad. That's the right side of the page.
Your akka,
Leela

qa.a: Splitting the page into what she controls and what she doesn't let Leela pour effort into recipes and the price board instead of a lucky dupatta.

qa.a: Seema might stop spending energy on things out of reach and feel less guilty when luck goes the other way.

Thirty rejections, Gautam. That's the number people always ask me about. Honestly, I nearly didn't get through them. For months I blamed myself for every no, and I also started doing odd things: the same blue kurta, the same pen, left foot first into every office lobby.
Then my mother asked me something simple. "Jaya beti, which part of an interview is actually yours?" So I made two lists. Mine: preparation, my portfolio, practising answers aloud, a polite follow-up. Not mine: how many people applied, the panel's mood, whether a hiring freeze came in.
I dropped the kurta business and put those hours into mock interviews with friends. I still got rejections. But when one came, I asked: did I do my part? If yes, I let it go.
The first offer came in month seven.

qa.q: What did Jaya's mother ask her?
qa.a: "Jaya beti, which part of an interview is actually yours?"

qa.q: How did Jaya feel during the months she blamed herself for every no?
qa.a: She felt anxious and responsible for everything, which is why she grabbed at rituals like the blue kurta for a sense of control.

qa.q: What choice did Jaya make after writing the two lists?
qa.a: She dropped the kurta and pen rituals and put those hours into mock interviews, the part she actually controlled.

qa.q: How might Gautam's listeners who are facing their own rejections hear Jaya's story?
qa.a: They might feel relief that a no isn't always their fault, and take away a practical way to spend their effort.

grounding: A young woman sorts interview outcomes into what she controls and what she doesn't, and drops lucky rituals and self-blame.

Saturday
Today Aditi and I did a coin-toss contest on the balcony. Heads, she gets a biscuit; tails, I get one. It came heads FIVE times in a row! Aditi was jumping.
I said, "Now it HAS to be tails. It's my turn by law." I was so sure I bet her my two biscuits.

qa.a: He could write down lots of tosses and look at what comes after every run of heads, to see whether tails is really due.

qa.q: How did the contest feel for Aditi?
qa.a: Aditi was jumping with joy at five heads, and winning Chirag's two biscuits as well must have made it a lucky day. 😊

Under the neem tree near the bus stand, Siddharth and Pradeep were tossing a one-rupee coin to decide who would bat first in their evening game. Pradeep kept calling heads and kept winning. Five heads in a row.
"Sixth time, I'm calling tails," Siddharth announced, rolling up his sleeves. "It's overdue. The coin will want to balance."
Pradeep grinned. "Coins don't want anything."
"Everything evens out. Dadi says so about the rain too."
The coin spun, flashed in the sun, and landed in the dust. Heads.
Siddharth stared at it. "Then it must be tails next. Definitely."
Pradeep had already picked up the bat.

qa.a: Who would bat first in their evening game.

qa.q: Why does Siddharth feel tails is 'overdue'?
qa.a: Siddharth feels confident because he believes things even out, as Dadi says about the rain, so five heads feel like a debt the coin must repay. 🤔

qa.q: After the sixth heads, what could help Siddharth see that each toss starts fresh?
qa.a: He could ask himself why the coin would remember the last five, or the two could toss many times and see heads and tails come in uneven runs.

qa.q: How does Pradeep see the five heads?
